Over the past decade, ethanol has represented the largest share of the biofuels market. Renewable diesel, a drop-in fuel, experienced tremendous growth in capacity and consumption in recent years due to the conversion of existing refineries. Biodiesel’s contribution has largely remained at a similar level, with a slight decrease in recent years, likely due to the growth of the renewable diesel market and demand for feedstock. Ethanol remains the top contributor to the bioeconomy. Data for advanced biofuels were obtained from the EPA’s public Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) data and were based on volume. Other advanced biofuels include biogas, butanol cellulosic diesel, cellulosic gasoline, cellulosic heating oil, naphtha, renewable heating oil, RNG, and renewable jet fuel (EPA’s term for SAF). This dataset includes small volumes of imported advanced biofuels. The following sections cover multiple biofuel topics, including policies that impact the market, feedstocks, and detailed sections on SAF, renewable diesel, biodiesel, ethanol, and RNG. 2.1 Biofuels Industry Drivers The following is a summary of significant factors impacting biofuels markets. Ethanol is an important component of the gasoline market, as 98% of gasoline is blended with 10% ethanol (Alternative Fuels Data Center 2025b). The majority of the gasoline component shipped from refineries is 84 sub-octane fuel, and blending it with ethanol brings it to 87 octane fuel of regular gasoline. 3 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. snollaG noilliM Other Advanced Biofuels Renewable Diesel Biodiesel Ethanol A primary market driver for U.S. biofuels production and consumption is the Renewable Fuel Standard. The RFS originated with the Energy Policy Act of 2005 and expanded under the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 (U.S. Congress 2007). The RFS established biofuels volumes increasing annually and provided the EPA with the authority to adjust required volumes based on availability. While the legislated volumes were through 2022, the EPA is responsible for establishing volume standards for each year. The RFS program assigns obligated parties (fuel refiners and importers) a renewable volume obligation each company is required to blend based on a percentage of the company’s total fuel sales. EPA manages and tracks the RFS through Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs). There are four overall RFS categories: (1) renewable fuel, which is largely satisfied by conventional corn grain ethanol; (2) advanced biofuel; (3) biomass-based diesel; and (4) cellulosic biofuel (EPA 2026a).4 Figure 3 illustrates how these RIN designations are nested in a way that allows fuels to meet more than one RFS category.
